studyName: NF1 Gene Rescue in Translational Animal Models
summary: The goal of this project is to test new technologies for correcting NF1 mutations at the genome or DNA level instead of current efforts that are focused largely on regulating targets in the NF1 signaling pathway. The proposal establishes a new collaborative team that brings together the expertise of two laboratories, each of which has established critical technologies and reagents on hand that provides a new approach for treating NF1. The Kesterson lab (UAB) has established several critical reagents for the study of NF1 including a newly created system to study NF1 by having a full-length NF1 cDNA that represents the key "coding" regions of the NF1 gene, which has all the critical information needed to produce the entire neurofibromin protein. His laboratory has also created the first mice and rats that have mutations in their NF1 gene that completely mimic those seen in patients. The Zhou lab (Yale) has developed key technologies based on "nanoparticles" for delivery of large size DNA like NF1, or for gene-editing reagents known as CRISPR/Cas9 that can correct mutations at the DNA level. This project proposes to conduct needed pre-clinical studies in NF1 relevant animal models to assess the ability to use nanoparticles to 1) deliver the cDNA that will then make neurofibromin protein, and 2) deliver the gene-editing reagents to directly correct the mutation causing NF1. Rats will also be created that carry NF1 patient mutations and characterize those for tumor formation and cognitive deficits. Rats are well known in the neuroscience field as the preferred species to assess cognitive and behavioral function. The ability of the nanoparticles to treat anticipated cognitive and behavioral deficits in the rats with NF1 mutations will be tested as well. If successful, the new systems will provide essential pre-clinical data and lay the foundation for clinical trials using nanomedicine to treat NF1 disease.

studyName: NF1 RNA Repair Based on Therapeutic Ribozymes
summary: The 1989 Nobel Prize in Chemistry went to Thomas R. Cech and Sydney Altman for their discovery of ribonucleic acid (RNA) molecules with catalytic properties similar to those of protein enzymes, leading to the term 'ribozymes'. Cech and colleagues studied a specific ribozyme, an intron of a gene in Tetrahymena thermophila, a single-celled organism. Ribozymes of its kind can be modified to specifically bind to a target RNA of choice, split this RNA at a specific site into two parts, and replace one part with another RNA sequence that is attached to the ribozyme. This so-called trans-splicing ability of engineered ribozymes establishes a potential strategy for therapeutic RNA repair: The faulty part of RNA that resulted from a genetic mutation in its associated gene is removed and replaced by the correct part. Such a repaired transcript then translates into fully functional proteins. Early proofs of this concept demonstrated repair of defective RNAs involved in cancer (p53), myotonic muscular dystrophy (DMPK) and sickle-cell anemia (beta-globin). This proposal builds upon this concept: Bioengineered trans-acting ribozymes are used to target faulty transcripts of the NF1 gene that carry mutations causing neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1). The aim is to effectively and specifically restore function to the NF1 gene product for a variety of patient-derived NF1 mutations in human cell lines. As part of the ribozyme design, potential obstacles on the path to NF1 clinical application will be considered and analyzed, including delivery of the therapeutic ribozymes, avoidance of off-target effects, and minimization of a possible immune response. By developing NF1 mouse models with patient specific mutations that are amenable to ribozyme-mediated correction we will prepare for subsequent animal studies, a necessary step prior to clinical testing. We envision our research to constitute the first step towards a novel RNA-based therapy for the treatment of NF1.

studyName: Investigating Synthetic Lethality Associated with NF1 Loss
summary: Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) is a genetic disease caused by a mutation of NF1, a gene which normally limits cell proliferation. NF1 patients initially have one of the two NF1 alleles which remains normal but is prone to become inactivated. When this occurs, benign tumors called neurofibromas develop and cause various health complications. In some cases, neurofibromas transform into aggressive life-threatening tumors. Initial identification of the NF1 gene as causative for the disease created hope that the defect could be corrected using gene therapy strategies. However, genetic correction of NF1 mutations is met with several outstanding issues that render this type of approach unlikely to succeed for the time being. Instead of trying to correct the disease causing-mutation, this project proposes a new approach to treat NF1 that aims at killing cells that have inactivated both copies of the NF1 gene. The concept underlying this original therapeutic approach is based on the fact that mutation of one gene often creates vulnerabilities towards inactivation of other genes that are not normally required for cell survival. A spinoff of the recently developed CRISPR/CAS9 technology will be used to identify genes that become essential for the survival of cells that have inactivated both copies of the NF1 gene. The focus will then move to target genes for which an FDA-approved drug is already available. Such a drug, if successful in killing NF1-mutant cells, should quickly become available for clinical testing in NF1 patients.

studyName: Development of Mutation Suppression Therapy in a Swine Model of NF1
summary: One in five Neurofibromatosis Type 1 (NF1) patients have a specific type of mutation in the NF1 gene that causes its protein production machinery to stop early, resulting in a shortened and usually non-functional product. There is a type of drug called a "nonsense mutation suppressor" that restores full-length production of protein in genes that have these mutations. These drugs are being developed for diseases like Cystic Fibrosis and Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy, and many clinical trials are underway for these patients. Unfortunately, the immense impact these drugs could have on NF1 patients with these mutations has yet to be explored. The goal of this proposal is to investigate the potential of nonsense mutation suppression therapies in NF1 patients. This group has developed a minipig model of NF1 that shows many of the clinical signs seen in human patients of NF1, including cafe-au-lait spots, dermal neurofibromas, and optic pathway glioma, and it has been used to find drugs that are both safe and effective in our preclinical model that can better inform researchers and clinicians before these drugs go into clinical trials in NF1 patients. Here, this project aims to develop a new swine model of NF1 with a slightly different mutation that will be suitable for testing these nonsense mutation suppression therapies. The preclinical utility of these drugs will be established with the goal of initiating a clinical trial in NF1 patients with a drug that is safe, tolerable, and effective in restoring NF1 gene function. The NF1 pig model developed in this proposal is expected to develop tumors similar to those found in human patients and can be used to establish the ability of these novel therapies to both eradicate the underlying genetic abnormality and cure existing manifestations of the condition in people living with NF1.

studyName: Exon skipping to treat Neurofibromatosis Type 1 (NF1) mutations
summary: Most currently available drugs to treat Neurofibromatosis Type I (NF1) are targeted at tumors; and as with many chemotherapies, they tend to have toxic side effects. Newer, less toxic therapies are needed. Antisense directed gene therapy, and more specifically exon skipping, is a successful therapeutic strategy for other diseases including Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) which also affects children. Antisense directed gene therapy causes cells to "skip" over faulty pieces of the genetic code, leading to a truncated but still functional protein despite the genetic mutation. Antisense oligonucleotides (AONs) are short synthetic modified nucleic acids that bind RNA through base pairing and enable modulation of its expression. The project hypothesizes that antisense directed gene therapy can be utilized to treat NF1 and is designed to test that possibility. Exons, the coding part of genes, within the NF1 transcript that may be skipped and still maintain gene function must be identified. The first aim is to create copies of the NF1 gene that are missing these prioritized exons and test their function in cell-based molecular assays. Next, antisense oligonucleotides will be designed and tested. This will involve computer-aided sequence analysis of the NF1 genomic region and the design of NF1 antisense phosphonodiamidite morpholino oligomers (PMOs) that target specific exons. These PMOs will be tested in normal cells for their exon-skipping efficiency. Human cell lines that have deleterious, patient-specific NF1 mutations will also be created using CRISPR/Cas9 technology to edit the genome. These mutations will occur within exons that have been shown to maintain gene function after deletion. PMOs that are efficacious will be moved forward and be tested in dose response for exon skipping efficiency in cells containing patient mutations. NF1 function will also be evaluated. Finally, mice models will be created, and the phenotypes characterized such that they may be used to show proof-of-Principal that exon skipping could be therapeutic for NF1. Ideally, exon skipping could be used clinically to treat NF1 patients that harbor mutations in non-critical regions of the gene. Production of even partially functional NF1 could help ameliorate phenotypes. This project will make the following three contributions to advancing the field of NF research. First, we will determine if exon skipping strategies are even a possibility for treating NF1. Second, data generated will direct future structure-function studies and possibly help lead to a "mini-NF1" gene cassette for gene replacement therapies. Finally, generation of mutant human cell lines and mice provides a resource for many other projects.

studyName: AAV, Zinc Finger Protein and Antisense Oligonucleotide Strategies for Restoration of Neurofibromin Expression
summary: Neurofibromatosis type I (NF1) is a genetic disorder caused by mutations in the neurofibromin gene. Patients with NF1 suffer from a variety of health challenges, including skin lesions, benign and malignant tumors of the optic and peripheral nervous system, and cognitive deficits. Current treatment options are limited and do not address the primary genetic defect associated with this disorder, namely the reduction in levels or complete loss of the neurofibromin protein within affected tissues. This project seeks to develop therapeutics that will directly address this core deficit in NF1 patients. The central focus is to develop two new NF1 drug candidates that will be ready for Pre-IND discussions with the FDA at the end of the third year of study. This ambitious goal will be achieved by developing and characterizing multiple potential therapeutics in parallel and analyzing them on common platforms in a joint scientific effort spanning fourteen clinical and basic science research laboratories. During the first two years of the project, the efficacy of different therapeutic modalities will be evaluated first in cell culture and then in mouse models of NF1. In year three, we will focus exclusively on the two most promising therapeutic strategies, advancing them through more intense efficacy and safety studies in NF1 mouse models to produce datasets that will be necessary for discussions with the FDA intended to prepare for trials of the drug candidates in patients.

studyName: Neuroprotection and optic nerve regeneration in a mouse NF1 OPG model
summary: Neurofibromatosis Type I (NF1) occurs at a frequency of 1/3000 worldwide and can cause non-cancerous tumor growth in the peripheral and central nervous systems. 15-20% of people with NF1 develop optic pathway gliomas (OPGs) in the first 7 years of life due to an excessive proliferation of astrocytes (support cells of the nervous system) and the invasion of tumors with microglia (resident immune cells in the nervous system). Retinal ganglion cells (RGCs), the nerve cells that send visual information from the eye to the brain, are vulnerable to the effects of aberrant astrocytes and microglia, and undergo cell death in many patients with OPGs, resulting in an irretrievable loss of vision. The objectives of this research are to prevent RGCs from dying in cases in which NF1-associated OPGs are diagnosed at an early stage of progression, or to enable remaining RGCs to regenerate connections back to the brain in cases in which OPGs are diagnosed at a more advanced stage and axons have atrophied. Several treatments that have proven to be successful in preserving injured RGCs and/or enabling RGCs to regenerate dam-age nerve fibers in earlier studies from our lab and others will first be tested individually for beneficial or possible negative effects in a mouse model of NF1-associated OPG. Therapies that prove to be benign or beneficial will then be combined and tested in larger groups in early and later stages of OPG progression in mice. In more basic research, we will investigate how 3 newly discovered pathways that regulate RGC survival interact with each other to develop better treatments for OPGs. Finally, we will work with the cell replacement groups to develop methods to enable endogenous or exogenous stem cell-derived RGCs to extend nerve fibers that can convey visual information to the brain. Our overall goal is to devise therapies that can be moved into clinical practice to improve vision in NF1 patients with OPGs.

studyName: Axon regeneration and vision restoration in NF1 OPG
summary: In optic glioma (OPG), including that associated with Neurofibromatosis type-1 (NF1), retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) sustain axon injury and patients lose vision, often in early life. Injury to RGC axons in the optic nerve, whether compressive, traumatic, ischemic or degenerative in nature, results in an irreversible loss of vision due to the inability of RGCs to remain viable and to regenerate their axons. Seminal studies in rodents over the past 2 decades have identified strategies that allow many RGCs to survive long-term after optic nerve injury and enable some RGCs to regenerate axons from the eye to the brain. Most of these data were developed in acute trauma models of optic nerve crush, which may or may not be directly translatable to the axon damage and optic nerve environment in NF1 OPG. In light of these promising results, we believe that the time is right for a collaborative group of investigators to join forces to achieve unprecedented levels of regeneration and to translate these findings into proof-of-concept in NF1 OPG models as well as a larger animal model, as an essential step towards eventual treatment of NF1 OPG patients.

studyName: Optimizing strategies to improve visual recovery from NF1 optic glioma
summary: Children with Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) are prone to the development of benign brain tumors that affect the optic pathway (optic gliomas) and result in vision loss. While current chemotherapy is effective at halting tumor growth, few patients regain vision. For this reason, it is imperative to identify new treatments that prevent or restore vision loss from these tumors. Research over the past 15 years in the Gutmann laboratory has demonstrated that mice engineered with Nf1 gene mutations develop optic gliomas and tumor associated vision loss. In the current GVRI proposal, we plan to use a novel discovery strategy to identify a core molecular signature of vision recovery following treatment in mice, and employ these findings to evaluate promising candidates in preclinical studies in genetically engineered mice with optic gliomas and vision loss. Leveraging the GVRI team science paradigm, discoveries made using these mice will be validated in other experimental paradigms developed in the Reh, Zack, and Young laboratories. In addition, novel findings emanating from other team efforts will be evaluated in these Nf1 optic glioma mice. Taken together, we aim to identify targeted therapeutic strategies that prevent or ameliorate vision loss in children with NF1 associated optic pathway gliomas.

studyName: New strategies of protecting RGCs and promoting optic nerve regeneration
summary: Vision loss associated with some patients of neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) is characterized by degeneration of the optic nerve and the loss of retinal ganglion cells (RGCs), following optic pathway glioma (OPG). Currently there is no solution to reverse the optic pathway damage and restore vision. Tremendous progress in both NF1/OPG and RGC biology provide an unprecedented opportunity of tacking this issue and developing relevant therapeutic strategies. The objective of this proposed study is to leverage our expertise in studying RGC survival and regeneration to explore novel neuroprotective and restorative approaches for NF1/OPG. As to protective therapies, we will assess the effects of available axon-protecting manipulations in NF1/OPG and also identify novel protective interventions targeting the vulnerability of RGCs of NF1/OPG. In addition, we will collaborate with exogenous cell replacement groups in developing a set of manipulations that maximize the extents of axon growth, so that transplanted RGCs could reach their targets for vision restoration. As a component of GVRI team, these proposed studies are expected to contribute to the development of vision restoration therapies for NF1/OPG patients.

studyName: Structural and functional restoration of the visual system in NF1
summary: The purpose of this proposal is to understand the specific barriers to visual system function and optic pathway regeneration in people suffering from Neurofibromatosis 1 (NF1) and to develop strategies to overcome those barriers. Previous work from our lab and others has shown (in animal models) that the mammalian visual system has the capacity to regenerate after injury, provided that the proper stimulus (or combination of stimuli) is provided. The cellular, molecular, structural and functional conditions leading to vision loss in the optic pathway of NF1 patients are unique. Thus, it is absolutely crucial to gain thorough understanding of these features in animal models of NF1 in order to develop viable strategies for curing vision loss in NF1 patients. This proposal outlines a strategy to define the optic eye-to-brain pathway in NF1 mutant mice and the specific structural and molecular barriers that must be overcome in order for optic axon regeneration to occur at different stages of the disease. We will test the efficacy of enhancing retinal neural activity on regeneration in NF1 mutants, and the impact of increasing specific cell growth pathways alone or in combination with activity augmentation. Using state-of-the-art tools, we propose to assess retinal axon regeneration, tumor growth and stability and recovery of visual function. Successful completion of these studies should greatly inform our understanding of visual defects in NF1 and strategies to reverse and overcome them.

studyName: Generation and neuroprotective studies of NF1 patient-derived RGCs
summary: Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) is the most common genetic condition in which individuals carrying the mutation are predisposed to develop a variety of types of tumors. Approximately 20% of children with NF1 mutations will develop tumors of the nerve that carries visual information from the eye to the brain, so called optic pathway gliomas (OPGs). NF1 OPGs can cause permanent vision loss ranging from a mild decline in visual acuity to complete blindness. Up to 50% of children with NF1 OPGs will suffer vision loss, typically between 1 to 8 years of age, which has a significant lifelong impact on the child's overall health and quality of life. Enhancing and restoring visual function in children with NF1 OPGs could dramatically improve their lifelong quality of life.Vision loss from NF1 OPGs ultimately results from damage to and loss of the retinal ganglion cells (RGCs), the retinal neurons that carry visual information from the eye to the brain. Since mammalian RGCs do not regenerate, it is important to develop approaches that maintain the health of a patient's remaining RGCs, so as to reduce or prevent additional vision loss. It is the goal of our work, which is part of the Gilbert Vision Restoration Initiative (GVRI), to use RGCs derived from human stem cells to better understand how NF1 mutations lead to RGC damage and cell loss and to develop strategies to promote RGC survival and function. NF1 RGCs will be generated from small skin biopsy or blood samples from patients with NF1 mutations. These patient derived cells will then be studied in our and other labs lab to uncover how their mutations affect the RGCs, and then we will test thousands of small molecules to try to identify ones that can reverse the effect of the NF1 mutation. It is hoped that these studies will lead to the development of potential drugs to preserve the vision of patients suffering from Neurofibromatosis type 1.

studyName: RGC differentiation and transplantation for NF1 OPG
summary: What regulates neuronal growth and differentiation in the central nervous system (CNS)? The optic neuropathy and vision loss seen in optic glioma (OPG) in some cases associated with Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) is one such disease that afflicts the eye that leads to damage and eventual loss of retinal ganglion cells (RGCs). Once lost, RGCs are not replaced in humans or other mammals resulting in irreversible blindness. Transplantation of stem cell derived-RGCs could be a feasible approach to restore vision; however, little is known about how to promote RGC differentiation from stem cells (SCs), or whether stem cell derived-RGCs transplanted into an adult would be able to integrate into either intact or degenerating retinal circuits, particularly in the context of an NF1 patient's retina. Thus, identifying the relevant signaling pathways that promote RGC specification will be necessary to generate donor RGCs that integrate and form functional connections within recipient retinas.Stem cell-based approaches provide new hope for the treatment of many neurodegenerative diseases. To date, several protocols have been reported for RGC generation from hiPSCs and hESCs, however these protocols are labor intensive, require significant time in culture, and yield only a few RGCs. To overcome these issues, we propose to utilize a rapid and direct induced RGC (iRGC) protocol modified from an induced neuron (iN) protocol established in an adjacent Stanford lab to investigate GDF, SoxC and other signaling on RGC fate specification in hiPSCs, with and without the NF1 background. The ultimate goal of this project will be to improve the efficiency of RGC differentiation from hiPSCs, and demonstrate efficacy of iRGC transplant with anatomic and functional assays, with attention to NF1 mutation in the donor iRGC population, and in the recipient host mouse.

studyName: Stem cell derived RGCs: Improving the success of transplantation strategies
summary: Our overall goal is to improve the success of RGC transplantation, using mouse cells, together with tissue engineering and pig to pig transplantation studies. We will first identify and optimize key variables using mouse cells that can be applied for pig, non-human primate and human retinal ganglion cell precursors. The premise is that the development of RGCs from stem cells is conserved and the cues we identify may be relevant for all RGCs. Testing them in mouse has two key advantages: The timeframe for differentiation is much shorter, which allows one to test more variables; and the mouse model allows for mouse to mouse (allograft) studies which is a likely therapeutic strategy in humans. We have shown that mouse stem cells-derived RGCs are diverse, functional and integrate into healthy and RGC-depleted retinas following injection into the chamber of the eye in front of the retina. We have also demonstrated long-term survival and growth of processes into the optic nerve. We have three sub-aims for this approach: 1 ) Identifying the stage of differentiation with the highest potential for transplantation 2. Evaluate different types of RGCs for transplantation studies 3. Improving RGC maturation in retinal tissue, differentiated from stem cells. We will work closely with team members to develop appropriate differentiation (DZ) and transplantation (JG) protocols.We will also develop novel tissue engineered transplants aimed at improving graft success. Using cells and protocols from Aim 1, we will develop polymer composite grafts capable of improving survival, engraftment, and differentiation of transplanted RGCs. Cells from JG and DZ, along with cells from Aim 1 will be used for these studies. Lastly, building upon studies by team members using mouse and human RGCs, we will develop pig RGCs for the purpose of performing pig-pig allograft (same species) studies in disease models. Human and mouse protocols from DZ and PB will be used to generate pig RGCs.

studyName: Human stem cell-derived RGCs for optic nerve regeneration
summary: Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) is the most common genetic condition in which individuals carrying the mutation are predisposed to develop a variety of types of tumors. studyName: Retina regeneration in zebrafish-Endogenous RGC replacement
summary: NF1 is a disease resulting from reduced levels of neurofibromin 1 that functions as a tumor suppressor. One in five children with NF1 have optic nerve tumors that can lead to retinal ganglion cell death and blindness. One approach for treating NF1-related blindness is to regenerate retinal ganglion cells from endogenous stem cells. Because zebrafish use endogenous stem cells to regenerate retinal ganglion cells, we propose that understanding this process in fish will inform us of strategies for stimulating a similar process in humans. With this goal in mind, we aim to identify gene expression changes and small molecules that are sufficient to drive retina regeneration in zebrafish and test their effect on retina regeneration in mammals.

studyName: Factors that promote ganglion cell regeneration
summary: Currently, there are no effective therapies to replace degenerated neurons in patients with retinal ganglion cell loss from optic pathway glioma (OPG), such as occurs in patients with Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1). By contrast, retinas of non-mammalian vertebrates, such as fish and amphibians, show a robust regenerative response following retinal damage. Upon injury to the retina, fish Muller Glia generate all different types of retinal neurons to replace those that were lost. There has been considerable progress in understanding the molecular mechanisms of regeneration in non-mammalian vertebrates, and if this knowledge could be applied to humans, it might lead to the development of new types of regenerative therapies for patients with impaired vision from Neurofibromatosis type 1. We have recently found that by expressing a key regulatory gene called Ascl1 in the Muller glia of mice, we can induce them to regenerate new neurons after injury to the ganglion cells. The new regenerated neurons in the mouse retinas wired up with the existing, undamaged neurons and became functional. These results showed for the first time that functional neuron regeneration is possible in mammals, like ourselves. We would like to apply these findings to patients; unfortunately not all types of retinal neurons were regenerated in the mouse retina, and one of the types of neurons that they do not regenerate is the ganglion cell, precisely the cell type lost in NF1 patients. Therefore, we propose to figure out what is missing that would allow the Muller glia of mice to make new ganglion cells, by developing novel screening methods to identify these factors. This proposal outlines a series of pilot experiments that will help ensure that the factors we identify in these screens are particularly relevant for NF1 patients.

studyName: Identification and functional characterization of the substrates of LZTR1 (schwannomatosis)
summary: LZTR1 is a substrate adaptor protein of the CUL3 ubiquitin ligase complex whose substrates and cellular functions remain mostly unknown. Our laboratory reported for the first time that human brain tumors harbor somatic mutations of the LZTR1 gene. Later studies revealed that LZTR1 is somatically mutated across many types of human tumors. Furthermore, mutations of LZTR1 were identified as the causal event leading to a significant number of cases of schwannomatosis. Schwannomatosis is a rare form of Neurofibromatosis that has only recently been identified. The genetic disorder affects less than 1 in 40,000 people, and causes the development of schwannomas on cranial, spinal and peripheral nerves. Schwannomas may cause pain that may be hard to manage. Although the causal tumor suppressor role of LZTR1 as genetic basis of schwannomatosis has been firmly established, the mechanism by which loss of the activity of the LZTR1 ubiquitin ligases triggers tumor development remains elusive. Temporally coordinated destruction of key cell regulatory proteins by the Ubiquitin-Proteasome System (UPS) represents an important control mechanism to ensure that specific protein functions are turned off at the right time, in the right compartment, and in a unidirectional fashion. Cullin/Ring/Ligase complexes (CRL) control the proteolysis of many important cell regulators. In humans, there are approximately 200 CRL ligases, each characterized by a different substrate recognition subunit that provides specificity by directly recruiting the substrates. Cullin-3 is the molecular scaffold of a major class of CRLs that use BTB domain proteins as substrate-specific adaptors. Despite their large number, only a handful of BTB domain proteins have well-established substrates and their biological functions are largely unknown. Recently, RAS and Rit1 have been proposed as potential substrates of LZTR1. In the context of this work, it was suggested that LZTR1 may inhibit MAPK pathway by repressing RAS activity, but the mechanism of RAS inhibition remains controversial. Furthermore, the full scope of LZTR1 substrates and cellular functions remain unknown.  Here, we will elucidate the normal biochemical and biological functions of LZTR1 and substrates and the mechanisms by which LZTR1 suppresses tumor growth. This work will use state of the art proteomics to identify and demonstrate the significance of crucial LZTR1 substrates in the context of cancer cells driven by LZTR1 inactivation. We anticipate that the proteomic-based discovery of new LZTR1 substrates will provide a major advance in our understanding of the links between ubiquitin ligases, tumor suppression and of the pathogenesis of Schwannomatosis and the many sporadic tumors driven by loss-of-function genetic alterations (mutations and deletions) of LZTR1. We postulate that LZTR1 substrates implement oncogenic functions that are normally restrained by LZTR1-mediated ubiquitin-dependent degradation. The expected overall impact of this innovative grant application is that it will fundamentally advance our mechanistic understanding of the LZTR1 ubiquitin ligase as genetic driver of schwannomatosis and sporadic tumors and lay the foundation for the optimization of new therapeutic strategies in syndromic and sporadic tumors associated with loss-of-function genetic alterations of LZTR1.

studyName: Hexokinase 2 displacement from mitochondria-associated membranes as a new antineoplastic approach in NF1-related tumors
summary: The metabolic rewiring of NF1-related tumor types is emerging as an important feature of their development and progression towards malignancy, but it remains poorly described, hampering the possibility to develop selective and innovative anti-neoplastic approaches. I have recently focused my attention on a key component of the metabolic machinery of tumor cells, hexokinase 2 (HK2). HK2 induction in diverse neoplastic models is well-characterized, as well as its correlation with disease progression, malignancy and resistance to chemotherapeutics. I have recently developed an anti-neoplastic approach targeting HK2, which efficiently and specifically kills tumor cells by displacing HK2 from the interface between endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria, where I have found HK2 localizes in neoplastic cells. This strategy is based on the use of a modular and flexible cell penetrating peptide, which is effective both in vitro and in vivo. In the present project, I am planning to specifically targeting HK2 in PN and MPNST cell models, which constitutes per se an unprecedented approach. To this aim, I will carefully evaluate the effect of the peptide and of peptide variants tailored on the features of the tumor and of its intracellular environment (e.g., extracellular protease composition) on the neoplastic growth in different tumor models, encompassing PN and MPNST cells, both in vitro and after xenograft injection in nude mice, and genetic mouse models of MPNST development.

studyName: Impact of PRC2 loss on Glutamine metabolism in MPNSTs
summary: Malignant Peripheral Nerve Sheath Tumors (MPNSTs) are aggressive, highly metastatic sarcomas that are in desperate need of new therapeutic approaches. Loss-of-function mutations in the histone methyltransferase Polycomb Repressive complex 2 (PRC2) are found in 60% of MPNSTs. Cancer-specific metabolic vulnerabilities represent unique therapeutic targets, and several metabolic inhibitors are entering clinical trials. However, MPNST metabolism is not well-studied, and the impact of PRC2 loss on MPNST metabolism is unknown. Given the potential benefit of targeting metabolic pathways in cancer and the increasing emphasis on metabolic inhibitors in treating NF1-deficient tumors, there is a critical need to explore the impact of PRC2 loss on MPNST metabolism. The overall goal of this project is to define the unique metabolic pathways that are disrupted in MPNSTs and to determine if these are actionable clinical targets. Our metabolomic profiling data identified the metabolite glutamine as significantly upregulated in PRC2-deleted MPNST cells. Additional studies demonstrate that treatment with the glutaminase inhibitor, CB-839, can attenuate growth of MPSNT cells with wildtype PRC2, but can accelerate growth of MPNST cells with PRC2 mutations. This data leads us to hypothesize that PRC2 loss is rewiring glutamine metabolism in MPNSTs. In Aim 1, we will examine glutamine metabolism pathways through in vitro growth assays with varying levels of key metabolic fuel sources. We will also analyze PRC2-dependent metabolic functions, including mitochondrial respiration and glycolysis using Seahorse assays and metabolite GC-MS tracing studies with metabolic inhibitors. In Aim 2, we will utilize our syngeneic orthotopic allograft MPNST model to determine the impact of PRC2 loss on in vivo efficacy of the glutaminase inhibitor CB-839. We will use a combination of pharmacological tools, CRISPR-Cas9 approaches and in vivo metabolite tracing to determine metabolic resistance mechanisms. These studies will define the impact of PRC2 on MPNST metabolism and examine the in vivo efficacy and metabolomic effects of the glutaminase inhibitor, CB839.

studyName: Malignant Peripheral Nerve Sheath Tumors Achilles Heel: Combinatorial Targeting of ERBB3 and Calcium Signaling
summary: This proposal will investigate the role that ErbB3 and calcium-mediated signaling pathways play in regulating cellular proliferation and survival by in malignant peripheral sheath tumors (MPNSTs). At present, there are no effective treatments for MPNSTs other than radical surgical resection. After resection, recurrence typically occurs and so patients with MPNSTs have abysmal survival rates. The pathogenesis of MPNSTs is driven by Ras hyperactivation, a result of NF1 loss, and the loss of other tumor suppressor genes such as p53, PTEN and CDKN2A that negatively regulate cell proliferation/survival. Clinically targeting hyperactive Ras and its effector molecules has failed and so there is a desperate need to identify new therapeutic targets. We have focused on identifying Ras- independent and -dependent signaling pathways necessary for MPNST proliferation and survival using comprehensive genomic analyses, kinase phospho-arrays, pharmacological screens and several animal models. Our efforts have identified ErbB3 (a receptor tyrosine kinase/RTK) and calmodulin (CaM) as potential therapeutic targets in MPNSTs. Although there is conflicting evidence that other RTKs can drive Ras hyperactivation in MPNSTs, the role of ErbB3 has not yet been investigated in MPNSTs. Interestingly, our transcriptomic analyses of NRG1? (an ErbB3 ligand) stimulated Schwann cells and our global shRNA screens implicate ErbB3 and calmodulin-mediated calcium signaling as key biological pathways driving MPNST proliferation. With the cumulative support of our screens and functional analyses, we hypothesize that simultaneous inhibition of NRG1? activated effector molecules and calmodulin regulated signaling pathways will cooperatively inhibit MPNST cellular proliferation and survival. In Aim 1, I will test the hypothesis that NRG1? activation of ErbB3 directly modulates calmodulin regulated signaling in MPNSTs to promote cellular proliferation and survival. In Aim 2, I will test the hypothesis that dual inhibition of the NRG1? effector, ErbB3, and calmodulin effector molecules induces a cytotoxic effect in MPNSTs. This work will yield novel information about MPNST tumorigenesis by investigating the role(s) of ErbB3 (an upstream activator of Ras) and calcium signaling pathways (which can be dependent or independent of Ras). My ultimate goal is to identify a novel combinatorial treatment for MPNSTs using FDA approved drugs or drugs that are already in clinical trials that can rapidly advance to clinical trials.

studyName: Mapping and Identifying the Roles of Protein Glycosylation in Neurofibromatosis 1
summary: Neurofibromin is a regulator of cancer driver proteins through its functional role as a Ras-GTPase activating protein. Upon loss-of-function mutations to neurofibromin, patients develop benign or malignant nerve sheath tumors that lead to the disease neurofibromatosis 1 (NF1), affecting 1 in 2,000 people. Due to the complex signaling network of neurofibromin and the cancer-driver pathways it regulates, phosphorylation post-translation modifications have been extensively studied to explain the biological mechanisms for tumor development. Protein glycosylation, specifically N-acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc), is known to have significant crosstalk with phosphorylation sites in the proteome, but has never been studied in the context of a living model system for potential regulation and contribution to the pathogenesis of NF1. To better characterize glycosylation changes at various stages of NF1 malignancies, this proposal aims to develop three complimentary chemical biology approaches to create tools for the understanding of protein GlcNAcylation in cellular model systems of NF1 and MPNSTs. We will use glycoproteomics to investigate how loss of neurofibromin affects O-GlcNAc incorporation in the proteome to reveal key sites of biological regulation affected by the Ras cancer driver pathway. We will also perform protein engineering on a N-acetylglucosamine transferase V (GnT-V), known to be overexpressed in malignant tumors, to identify protein substrates in non-malignant and malignant Schwann cells. Revealing the substrate scope of GnT-V will allow the identification of biological pathways that are aberrant in malignant nerve cells due to increased glycosylation at specific glycosites. We will also biochemically investigate glycosylation marks directly on neurofibromin, to give a clearer picture of how post-translational modifications affect the interaction of neurofibromin with cancer driver proteins and affect neurofibromin localization.

studyName: The use of novel YAP/TEAD Hippo pathway inhibitors to target Merlin (NF2) null tumors
summary: Currently, surgical resection of schwannoma and meningioma tumors is the mainstay of their treatment with the associated risks of damaging neighboring nervous system tissue and the need for repeated surgeries in those with NF2. Research in Hippo pathway signaling and its role in driving tumor development has increased greatly in the last few years and the significance of this pathway has driven the development of new small molecule inhibitors to target this important signalling pathway. The novel YAP/TEAD inhibitors developed by Vivace are stable, orally available, show no apparent toxicity and demonstrate a potent effect in vitro to block the proliferation of two human tumor types, meningioma and schwannoma, both seen in individuals with NF2. In vivo, the compounds block TEAD activity in nervous system tissue, reducing TEAD expression and strongly inhibiting levels of the TEAD target CTGF in Schwann cells. The next and obvious step is to test these compounds using two well-characterized and well-used in vivo pre-clinical models for these two tumor types. Many NF2 patients will be affected by both schwannoma and meningioma tumors and the potential for the use of a single YAP/TEAD compound to treat both tumor types in an individual patient is particularly exciting. For all these reasons, we feel that this work has the potential to create a significant impact in the future treatment of both patients with NF2 as well as the large numbers of patients with sporadic schwannoma and meningioma tumours.  We propose to test the efficacy of novel Hippo pathway inhibitor to reduce the growth of Merlin-null schwannoma and meningioma tumor cells. A collaboration (established at the 2018 CTF meeting in Paris) with the company Vivace Therapeutics has allowed us to start testing in vitro the use of novel inhibitors of TEAD auto-palmitoylation to block tumour cell growth. All MTAs for their use have been signed and Vivace will support the running costs of the project outside of the salary costs provided in this grant. These inhibitors are non-toxic, can be given orally and are tolerated well in vivo, both in our work and in other Merlin-null tumor models. Analysis of TEAD protein expression in human tumour cells shows high heterogeneity in TEAD expression between different individual human tumors; the inhibitors we plan to use for our experiments will target the function of all 4 TEAD proteins. Our data in vitro using human primary schwannoma and meningioma tumor cells shows an effective block in tumor growth, even at low concentrations of 100nM and below .  Using the periostin-CRE / NF2fl/fl model of schwannoma , we have monitored cell proliferation in vivo both within DRG and within the cochlear nerve in these animals at 3 months of age and we can already see increased cellularity within the DRG tissue and cell proliferation within the cochlear nerve. Collaborations are in place to assist with both the use of the Postn-CRE-NF2fl/fl mouse model (Dr Charles Yates, Indiana University, USA) and analysis of mouse vestibulocochlear preps (Dr Dan Jagger, UCL Ear Institute, UK). Analysis of sciatic nerve tissue shows the effectiveness of one YAP/TEAD inhibitor used in vivo to reduce TEAD expression (an effect of reduced palmitoylation) together with a strong reduction of CTGF expression, a well-characterised TEAD-dependent target in cells.  The work in this proposal will also look to test whether these TEAD inibibitors may be used to target meningioma tumor growth in vivo using an orthotopic model of meningioma in the mouse. This work will be conducted in collaboration with Professor Christian Mawrin (University of Magdeburg, Germany), who is expert in such models. As described above, the proliferation of human meningioma tumour cells is also blocked by these YAP/TEAD inhibitors.  Two different YAP/TEAD inhibitors have been supplied to us by Vivace; both will block the activity of all TEAD proteins in cells and are well characterized in terms of their pharmacokinetics and lack of toxicity in vivo.  With this exciting pilot data and the use of in vivo schwannoma and meningioma mouse pre-clinical models, we will:  1. Test the effects of YAP/TEAD inhibition upon tumor growth in the PostnCRE-NF2fl/fl mouse model at 3, 5 and 9 months.  We will use different timescales of drug treatment (at 30mg/kg) followed by EdU injection and harvesting of tissue. Tissue can be analysed by EdU stain and/or H&E analysis of paraffin sections. At later timepoints, functional analysis (eg righting reflex) may be used to functionally measure vestibulocochlear function. For all experiments, as we have used previously, the PLP-GFP line will be bred onto the PostnCRE-NF2fl/fl background to allow identification of GFP-positive glial cells in our tissue analysis. This combined mouse line is already available in our new fully IVC animal facility.  2. Test the effects of YAP/TEAD inhibition upon tumor growth in an orthotopic mouse model of meningioma.  As shown in our prelimnary data, inhibition of YAP/TEAD function significantly decreases proliferation of human primary meningioma tumor cells. These compounds are also potently effective at reducing cell proliferation of meningioma cell lines as well in vitro (eg. BenMen1 and KT21 cells). Meningioma tumors are the most common intracranial tumor type and are common in patients with NF2.  We will use the well characterised convexity and skull base models to test the effectiveness of the YAP/TEAD inhibitors in blocking tumor growth. Currently genetic models of meningioma development (eg. prostaglandin D2 synthase driven CRE) do not allow for the testing of such compounds.  In these experiments we will use injection of meningioma cell lines (BenMen1, KT21) and monitor cell proliferation by EdU and analysis of samples by H&E staining with and without inhibitor dosing.  Through these two aims, this project will test whether these inhibitors may be suitable for clinical trials in the future.

studyName: Understanding the role of purinerigic signaling on tumor formation in a mouse model of Neurofibromatosis Type 1
summary: Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) is a disorder that affects 1:3,000 individuals worldwide. Loss of function of the neurofibroma gene (NF1) causes over activation of the RAS oncogenic signaling pathway. People with NF1 have an increased risk of developing tumors (neurofibromas), both benign and malignant anywhere along the peripheral nervous system (PNS). Neurofibromas arise from Schwann cells (SCs) and/or Schwann cell precursors (SCP). SCs support axons in the peripheral nervous system (PNS). To date, there is no cure for this disease. Therefore, the purpose of this proposal is to identify potential treatments for NF1 by studying the mechanisms involved in tumor formation.  To identify potential markers and therapeutic targets for NF1, we performed microarray analysis on human plexiform neurofibromas. We dissociated human neurofibromas and sorted tumor derived cells into SCs (p75+/EGFR-) and SCP tumor-initiating cells (p75+/EGFR+) (p75 marks neural crest cells, SC precursors, and non-myelinating SCs, and EGFR+ marks cells that express the Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor) [Schwann cells are EGFR negative]. The hypothesis behind the cell sorting is that genes expressed in neurofibroma SCP-tumor initiating cells (p75+/EGFR+) more than in differentiated neurofibroma Schwann cells (p75+/EGFR-) contribute to tumor initiation. From this microarray study, we found that a purinergic receptor, P2RY14 expression was increased in SCP-like tumor initiating cells (p75+/EGFR+). Then, we sorted the SCP tumor initiating cells (p75+/EGFR+) into P2RY14 positive or negative (p75+/EGFR+/P2RY14+ or p75+/EGFR+/P2RY14-) and we found that the p75+/EGFR+/P2RY14+ cells show an increased ability to self-renew and form spheres in vitro. These results suggest that tumor initiating cells (p75+/EGFR+) that are P2RY14+ might drive tumor growth.  To test if P2RY14 is tumor promoting in vivo, I bred our genetically engineered neurofibroma mouse model (Nf1 fl/fl DhhCre) to P2RY14 knockout mice (P2RY14-/-). Knocking out P2RY14 in the neurofibroma mice (P2Y14-/-; Nf1 fl/fl DhhCre) increases survival and reduces tumor number. This data demonstrates that P2RY14 is involved in neurofibroma formation and that knockout of this receptor in the neurofibroma mouse model increases survival rate in neurofibroma bearing mice.  I hypothesize that P2RY14 promotes neurofibroma growth by enhancing tumor cell self-renewal and/or proliferation in vitro and that inhibition of this receptor in vivo will result in a decrease of tumor growth. This hypothesis will be tested by completion of these specific aims:  Aim 1: Determine if the P2RY14 receptor is necessary for neurofibroma tumor cell proliferation in vitro. I hypothesize that P2RY14 signaling promotes neurofibroma growth in a cell autonomous way by regulating SCP proliferation and/or self-renewal in vitro. A) To determine if P2RY14 activation affects SCP cell proliferation, I will measure proliferating cell rates in WT and Nf1-/- SCP after addition of UDP (P2RY14 agonist). B) To determine if P2RY14 is necessary for neurofibroma SCP proliferation, I will silence P2RY14 expression in WT and Nf1-/- SCP in vitro using the P2RY14 pharmacological inhibitor and/or short-hairpin RNA (shRNA) and measure the rate of proliferating cells. If a change is found, I will determine if the change is MAPK dependent by monitoring RAS signaling or, determine if the change is P2RY14 dependent by monitoring cAMP levels.  Aim 2: Determine if the P2RY14 inhibitor drug can decrease neurofibroma growth. I will perform a drug study to determine if administration of a P2RY14 inhibitor by itself and/or in combination with the MEK inhibitor selumetinib for 7 days decreases cell proliferation, cell death, PKA and/or MAPK signaling. I will read out results by immunohistochemistry in tumor sections. If no change is found then, I will conclude that P2RY14 effects are mainly through tumor initiation. If an effect is seen, I will determine what cell types are involved in this process and increase the duration of the drug treatment to assess tumor size and tumor growth kinetics overtime.  Upon completion of the proposed aims in this grant, I will determine if P2RY14 is necessary for neurofibroma tumor cell proliferation in vitro and test if P2RY14 inhibition by drug delivery has an effect on tumor growth in vivo.  A critical gap in the field are the absence of mechanistic studies on the cause of tumor formation and the limited number of drugs available to treat NF1. Therefore, to fill this critical gap in knowledge, in Aim 1 I propose to determine if P2RY14 is necessary for neurofibroma cell proliferation in vitro. In Aim 2, I propose to determine if a P2RY14 pharmacological inhibitor can decrease neurofibroma growth.  Our results will impact the neurofibroma field not only by defining purinergic signaling mechanisms relevant to neurofibroma development but I will also establish if the P2RY14 inhibitor can be used as a treatment for NF1.

studyName: Unveiling the molecular mechanisms of neurofibromin regulation for therapeutic targeting in neurofibromatosis type 1
summary: Neurofibromatosis type 1 is one of the most common dominantly inherited genetic disorders, affecting approximately 1 in 3000 individuals, and is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the NF1 gene product, neurofibromin 1 (NF1). The clinical manifestations of neurofibromatosis type 1 exhibit significant heterogeneity but frequently patients develop learning difficulties, bone deformities and benign tumors of Schwann cells in the skin (dermal neurofibromas) and/or peripheral nerves (plexiform neurofibromas). These tumors can cause patients significant pain, disfiguration and functional impairment. Plexiform neurofibromas can develop in to malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors (MPNSTs), the most common malignancy occurring in neurofibromatosis type 1 patients, for which there are poor rates of survival and no effective approved treatments. Clearly, an understanding of NF1 biology at the molecular level is critical for the development of effective therapeutic strategies for patients with neurofibromatosis type 1.  Despite much effort over several decades, a robust molecular understanding of how NF1 is regulated is severely lacking. NF1 is as a RAS GTPase-activating protein (GAP) and negatively regulates RAS activation by stimulating hydrolysis of RAS bound GTP to GDP. Growth factors recruit guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs) such as SOS to promote GTP loading of RAS, and RAS-GTP then binds to several effectors to activate critical downstream signaling cascades, including RAF-MEK1/2-ERK1/2 signaling (MAP kinase pathway). Activation of RAS under normal circumstances is transient and tightly controlled, and we know from biochemical kinetic and genetic evidence that NF1�s ability to switch off RAS must itself be actively regulated. However, despite findings from our laboratory that NF1 forms a high-affinity homodimer, and also heterodimerizes with the negative regulator of RAS signalling SPRED1, our understanding of the processes by which NF1 is regulated remains very limited.  In this proposal we now present robust evidence that NF1 is directly phosphorylated by the ERK1 and ERK2 MAP kinases. We believe this observation is an important foundation for fundamentally furthering our molecular understanding of NF1 biology. We propose biochemical and genetic approaches to test the hypothesis that these phosphorylation events are a negative feedback loop to NF1 that might be critical for the normal switching off of RAS signaling that follows its activation. This would represent the first identified negative feedback loop to RAS-GAPs. If correct, we plan to determine the mechanisms by which ERK1/2 regulate NF1 using biochemical and genetically-engineered cell models. We also propose to test whether loss of such a negative feedback mechanism that permits the inappropriate hyperactivation of ERK1/2 and other RAS effectors might underlie MPNST development in neurofibromatosis type 1 in vivo models. Loss of a RAS-ERK-NF1 feedback mechanism could also explain why MEK1/2 inhibitors (MEKi), which are under priority review by the FDA, exhibit a therapeutic window and are effective for the treatment of plexiform neurofibromas, but in most sporadic cancers with RAS- MAPK mutations exhibit a narrow therapeutic window and consequently modest efficacy. An understanding of feedback regulation of NF1 by ERK1/2 would be invaluable for our understanding of how best to employ and schedule ERK1/2 pathway inhibitors, such as MEKi, in patients with neurofibromatosis type 1. This knowledge may also inform the development of alternative therapeutic strategies. Finally, unveiling mechanisms by which ERK1/2 regulate NF1 could also reveal how other cellular signals regulate NF1, such as those anticipated from receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs).

studyName: Predictive Modeling Utilizing a Preclinical NF1-MPNST Platform Suitable for Precision Oncology
summary: NF1 is one of the most prevalent cancer predisposition syndromes, affecting 1 in 2500 individuals worldwide. Approximately 10-13% of affected individuals will develop an aggressive sarcoma, the malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor (MPNST). One of the major barriers to the improving outcomes for these patients is the lack of preclinical models that accurately represent the genetic heterogeneity of these cancers. In this regard, no effective therapies have emerged from recent clinical trials, which likely reflects the use of a single mouse MPNST model system (Nf1+/-;Trp53+/- mice) and a paucity of human tumor xenografts. To address this critical problem, our laboratories have successfully generated a series of patient-derived MPNST xenografts that more accurately reflect the genetic heterogeneity seen in the human condition. To date, we have generated 15 NF1-MPNST patient-derived xenograft (PDX) lines propagated in immunocompromised mice. We have demonstrated that these lines harbor the spectrum of genomic alterations that we see in patients with NF1, including germline and somatic NF1 mutations, and subsets with loss of CDKN2A, TP53 mutations, EED/SUZ12 mutations, and numerous copy number changes. We plan to use collagen microtissues generated from the PDX lines in vitro to perform high throughput drug screening, to accelerate identification of efficacious therapeutic combinations. We will then proceed with in vivo testing of the promising combinations. This proposal brings together four institutions with deep expertise in NF1 research and a non-profit, collaborative research institute, Sage Bionetworks, to develop a truly integrated effort to explore the therapeutic potential of a set of well-vetted drugs for MPNST. Specific Scientific Aims Aim 1: Continue development and characterization of NF1-MPNST PDX lines to maintain the platform for pre-clinical testing. Our goal is to generate a total of at least 20 unique PDX lines available for use in Aims 2 and 3. Aim 2: Determine the in vitro response to cytotoxic chemotherapy or targeted therapy based on molecular phenotype and computational modeling. Our goal is to screen all PDX for responses to a set of well vetted candidate drugs and drug combinations using a novel high throughput 3-dimensional tissue culture platform. Aim 3: Determine the in vivo response to cytotoxic chemotherapy or targeted therapy or their combination and identify molecular signatures that are associated with this response.

studyName: TRAPping neurofibromas. Inhibition of the mitochondrial chaperone TRAP1 as an anti-neoplastic strategy for NF1-associated tumors
summary: Plexiform neurofibroma (PN) is a complex tumor that develops within perineural sheaths of nerve bundles in patients with neurofibromatosis type I (NF1), a tumor-predisposing genetic syndrome. Albeit benign, PNs can be disfiguring, can dangerously compress surrounding tissues or undergo transformation into highly aggressive sarcomas termed malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors (MPNSTs). PN formation and growth require the deregulated induction in Schwann cells of the Ras/ERK transduction axis that follows homozygous loss-of-function mutations at the NF1 gene, which encodes the Ras GTPase activating protein neurofibromin.Oncogenic signalling via the Ras/ERK pathway contributes to the metabolic rewiring of neoplastic cells, and mitochondria can play a promoter role in these changes, allowing cells to thrive in the conditions of limited oxygen supply they encounter during the neoplasm accrual. We have previously shown that Ras/ERK signalling has a mitochondrial branch in tumor cells. In NF1-related tumor cell models, hyperactive mitochondrial ERK enhances the activity of the molecular chaperone TRAP1. We have demonstrated that TRAP1 causes inhibition of succinate dehydrogenase (SDH), an enzyme placed at the crossroad between Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), increasing intracellular levels of the oncometabolite succinate, which in turn activates the pro-neoplastic programs of the transcription factor HIF1. Therefore, TRAP1 contributes to the pro-neoplastic metabolic rewiring of NF1-related tumor cells, and its genetic ablation abolishes tumorigenicity of MPNST cells in xenograft models.Taken together, these data indicate that TRAP1 is an interesting target for the development of anti-neoplastic compounds active on PNs and MPNSTs. In the framework of a previous CTF Drug Discovery Initiative, we have used innovative molecular dynamics approaches to identify pharmacophore pockets in the TRAP1 structure that can host small molecules with a potential activity as allosteric inhibitors of TRAP1 chaperone cycle. We have selected eleven compounds that inhibit TRAP1 activity in a very specific way, as they are not effective on its cognate chaperone Hsp90. These molecules revert TRAP1-dependent inhibition of SDH in MPNST cells and abrogate their in vitro tumorigenicity.Based on this solid ground of preliminary data, our present project aims at the in vivo assessment of the anti-neoplastic effect of TRAP1 inhibition. We will use a double-pronged approach: first, we will analyze wheter TRAP1-targeting compounds affect the xenografic growth of PN and MPNST cell models in nude mice; second, we will exploit a genetic mouse model of MPNST onset and growth, the Nf1flox/flox; p53flox/flox; PLP-CreERT2+ mouse in which both the Nf1 and the p53 locus can be selectively ablated in Schwann cell precursors, to investigate whether TRAP1 allosteric inhibitors can block or even revert the growth of these malignancies. We will then perform ex vivo experiments on tumor samples in order to determine their metabolic and biochemical features, and how TRAP1 blockade impacts on them.In collaboration with Giorgio Colombo, University of Pavia, Italy, we will also expand the panel of TRAP1 allosteric inhibitors. To this aim, we will utilize a molecular dynamics approach to to predict molecular scaffold derivatives of our panel of inhibitors that could display an increased inhibitory effect on TRAP1 chaperone and pro-neoplastic activity.Future developments of this proposal foresee the combined use of TRAP1 allosteric inhibitors with other anti-neurofibroma drugs, e.g. molecules targeting the Ras/ERK signalling pathway.Altogether, the experiments of the present application are intended to exploit the metabolic liabilities of PNs and MPNSTs, in order to extend the weaponry that can be used against these malignancies. TRAP1 allosteric inhibitors could constitute an innovative approach for the development of selective and effective anti-tumor drugs for NF1 patients.

studyName: Targeting the NRG1/ErbB signaling axes for the treatment of Schwannomatosis and associated pain
summary: Background: Patients with Schwannomatosis overwhelmingly present with intractable pain. The etiology of pain in Schwannomatosis is not clear, and there are no effective therapies that relieve Schwannomatosis pain. Schwannomatosis research is limited by the lack of established Schwannomatosis cell lines and animal models. Malignant cancer cells can grow indefinitely in cell culture and can form xenograft tumors in mice, which allows for the characterization of their growth and assessment of novel therapeutic drugs. However, as a benign tumor, Schwannomatosis tissues isolated from patients do not grow in culture. Therefore, developing a platform to study tumor-induced pain and identify novel strategies that relieve pain in patients with Schwannomatosis is a significant unmet need. In our preliminary studies, we have established patient-derived Schwannomatosis cell lines.By culturing Schwannomatosis cells in the DRG model, we found that Schwannomatosis cells secrete molecules that activate macrophages, which produce inflammatory cytokines and induce pain responses in the dorsal root ganglia. We performed RNASeq gene expression profiling study, and found that inflammatory pathways are activated and genes in the NRG-1/ErbB pathways are elevated in Schwannomas. We further found that schwannomas, via producing NRG1, activates ErbB receptor on tumor-associated macrophages to release inflammatory cytokines, and thus contributing to the development of neuropathic pain.Hypothesis: We hypothesis that Schwannomatosis tumor cells, via producing elevated levels of NRG-1, activate ErbB receptor on tumor-associated macrophages to induce inflammatory pain.Specific Aims: We propose to determine in:    Aim 1) determine the mechanisms of NRG1/ErbB signaling on pain response and tumor growth in DRG culture model;    Aim 2) determine the efficacy of NRG1/ErbB blockade on controlling pain and tumor growth in Schwannomatosis mouse model.Study Design: In Aim 1, we will use wide-spectrum ErbB tyrosine kinase inhibitors to block NRG-1/ErbB signaling in macrophages, and determine its effects on pain molecule expression in DRG slice culture model. In Aim 2, we will implant Schwannomatosis cells in the sciatic nerve model. We will treat mice with ErbB TKI to block NRG1/ErbB signaling, and evaluate its effects on tumor growth and pain response.

studyName: Experimental Therapeutic Evaluation of PSC5-6 using a pre-clinical Mouse Model of Neurofibromatosis Type 1
summary: Plexiform neurofibromas (PNs) are complex, precancerous, slow-growing tumors arising from large peripheral and cranial nerves in pateitns with neurofibromatsosi type 1 (NF1) and can cause severe morbidity including paralysis and death through their progressive compression of vital structures such as the spinal cord, the airway and vasculature. Currently, there is only one approved drug therapy (selumetinib) to treat plexiform neurofibromas in NF1 patients, and a significant subset of patients do not respond. Thus, novel therapeutic strategies to treat PNs are urgently needed. NF1 is caused by germline mutations in the NF1 tumor suppressor, which encodes a GTPase-activating protein (GAP) called neurofibromin that forms a molecular complex with activated Ras-GTP and increases Ras-GTP hydrolysis to the inactive GDP-bound conformation. When neurofibromin function is disrupted by genetic mutations, Ras activity become aberrantly increased, leading to tumorigenesis. Ras is at the apex of a series of signaling cascades, including the Ras-Raf-Mek-Erk, PI3K, and Rho pathways. Given the complexity of the downstream signaling pathways, the most ideal treatment strategy for NF1 is to reduce pathological activation of Ras signaling itself. However, due to its complex post translational modification and small binding pocket, it has been long regarded as a pharmacologically intractable target. Recently, however, next generation small molecular Rac inhibitors have entered development and have demonstrated considerable promise. PSC5-6 is a small molecular Ras inhibitor developed by Pisces Therapeutics, which has demonstrated activity in NF1 sarcoma (malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor) cell lines and additionally, in an animal model of another closely linked <U+FFFD>Rasopathy, <U+FFFD>Costell Syndrome. In this study, we will evaluate the tolerability, pharmacokinetic, and pharmacodynamic properties of PSC5-6 in a genetically engineered mouse model of NF1, and further, whether PSC5-6 can halt and/or prevent the progression of plexiform neurofibromas in a genetically engineered mouse model of NF1. PSC5-6 proves efficacious in this preclinical model, these studies will generate the data needed to catalyze the clinical translation of PSDC5-6 in an early phase trial in NF1 patients with plexifom neurofibroma who are refractory to currently available treatment modalities.

studyName: Exploiting macropinocytosis for therapeutic delivery to Nf2-deficient schwannoma cells
summary: Significance/RationaleThe benign, slow-growing nature of schwannomas presents unique challenges to therapeutic intervention, precluding the use of strategies that target rapidly dividing, metabolically active cells, and diminishing the therapeutic window for treatment. Recent work from the McClatchey lab, showed that merlin deficiency noticeably primes the membrane:cytoskeleton interface for growth factor-induced macropinocytosis, including in schwannoma cells. Mounting evidence suggests that beyond its physiological roles, macropinocytosis is also an important conduit for the delivery of therapeutic macromolecules into tumor cells. Since target cell entry is rate-limiting for many macro-therapeutics, tumor cells that are macropinocytosis-proficient may be particularly amenable to these promising strategies. Moreover, once internalized, macropinosomes merge with the endolysosomal system, and it is generally thought that slowing or impeding endolysosomal processing protects the contents from lysosomal degradation and enhances macro-therapeutic efficacy. The goal of this proposal is to evaluate the in vivo uptake of stapled peptides by Nf2-/- schwannoma cells via macropinocytosis. We will monitor the ability of Nf2-/- cells to internalize two fluorescently stapled peptides in vivo: one that mimics the BH3-domain of pro-apoptotic proteins to inhibit BCL2 family members and one that inhibits histone deacetylase (HDAC) family members. In addition to being the lead examples of this type of therapeutic strategy, both peptides have been tested in mouse models and BH3 mimetics have been extensively used in human clinical trials.Preliminary DataTo demonstrate that schwannoma cells of PeriostinCre;Nf2flox/flox DRG are primed for macropinocytosis, we performed an in vivo macropinocytosis uptake assay by intravenously (i.v.) injecting the fluorescently-tagged macro molecule FITC-Ficoll (70 kDa). DRGs were then dissected and further incubated in cell culture plates with the fluorescently-tagged TMR-Dextran. This two-step assay demonstrated that the Nf2-deficient cells in PeriostinCre;Nf2flox/flox DRGs are uptaking macromolecules from the extracellular medium and importantly that macromolecules injected intravenously are able to reach the DRG schwannomas.Aims    Specific Aim 1. To demonstrate specific macropinocytosis uptake in Nf2-deficient cells in vivo. We will test the hypothesis that Nf2-deficient vs normal cells preferentially take up stapled peptides in vivo via macropinocytosis. We will i.v. inject Nf2flox/flox control and Postn-Cre;Nf2flox/flox mutant mice with FITC-Ficoll to reveal cellular areas of macropinocytosis uptake. Comparison between Nf2-deficient tumor cells in DRG and Nf2-epxressing tissues like normal nerve roots or sciatic nerve will allow to demonstrate if the macropinocytosis uptake is specific to Nf2-deficient tumor cells.    Specific Aim 2. To optimize the delivery route and concentration of hydrocarbon stapled peptides to reach DRG schwannoma cells of Postn-Cre;Nf2flox/flox mice. We will test different dosages of fluorescently-tagged peptides (BIM-FITC and 16cyc-HxA-FITC) and two different delivery routes (intraperitoneal and tail vein injection) to evaluate the biodistribution of the stapled peptides in the Nf2-deficient cells of the DRGs and in Nf2-expressing tissues.    Specific Aim 3. To evaluate the efficacy of hydrocarbon stapled peptides in controlling the schwannoma cells proliferation in Postn-Cre;Nf2flox/flox mice. In this aim we will assess the effect of the two hydrocarbon stapled peptides (BIM and 16cyc-HxA) on tumor growth in the Postn-Cre;Nf2flox/flox mice.PerspectivesSuccessful completion of this studies will establish a new ex vivo assay for high throughput screening of drug compounds inhibiting macropinocytosis uptake in Nf2-deficient cells. Importantly, this ex vivo assay can be performed with both mouse and human schwannoma tissues. Complementary ex vivo analyses in human schwannoma tissue will help to further refine and optimize these novel strategies in advance of clinical testing. This proposal will provide a proof-of-concept for the use of two hydrocarbon stapled peptides and further studies will be able to test other macro-therapeutics (protein-conjugates, lipid nanoparticules, extravesicular vesicles or synthetic nanocarriers and exosomes based on the same model that NF2-deficient tumor cells and not normal cells are primed for macromolecules uptake.

studyName: TYK2 as a Biomarker and Therapeutic Target for NF1-Associated Malignant Peripheral Nerve Sheath Tumors
summary: The most common malignant cancer affecting people with neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) is the malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor (MPNST), a highly aggressive soft tissue cancer (sarcoma) that commonly develops from a benign precursor tumor. In this regard, 8%-13% of adults with NF1 will develop MPNSTs. Currently, there are no effective treatments for these cancers, and the vast majority of people with MPNST will die within 5 years of initial diagnosis.  Because these cancers arise from benign tumors, there is also a pressing need to be able to diagnose and distinguish true MPNSTs from non-cancerous precursors, which appear similar on advanced imaging studies such as MRI or PET scans. Using DNA sequencing technologies, we recently identified a frequently mutated gene in NF1-associated MPNSTs called TYK2. This mutation is not found in the benign precursors, however. Furthermore, in our previous experiments, we showed that mutations in this gene are critical for tumor cell survival, both in petri dishes and in tumors from mice.  Thus, we propose that TYK2 mutations drive tumor growth by preventing cell death. In this manner, TYK2 mutations may suggest a poor prognosis for those MPNSTs that harbor them. Furthermore, drugs that block the effects of TYK2 may prove to be useful in the battle against this aggressive cancer.  In this project, we aim to clarify the role of TYK2 in MPNST development and growth by performing experiments in previously engineered tumor cell lines in petri dishes as well as brand new tumor cells derived by our laboratory from patient samples and grown in mice. In addition, we will determine whether TYK2 mutations can reliably determine the likelihood of a poor prognosis or future tumor progression. Finally, we will assess whether drugs that block TYK2 prevent MPNST growth both in the petri dish and in mouse tumors. These experiments have the potential to lead to a markedly better treatment, which is desperately needed for these aggressive sarcomas.

studyName: Developing ELISA/IHC-Capable NF1 Monooclonal Antibody
summary: Neurofibromatosis Type 1 (NF1) is an autosomal dominant genetic disorder in which the amount of wild type neurofibromin produced by the remaining functional gene is a significant factor in the progression and severity of NF1 symptoms (i.e., haploinsufficiency driven). Given neurofibromin’s impact in regulating the Ras pathway and the importance of neurofibromin protein levels directly impacting many downstream pathways the availability of sensitive and specific antibodies to facilitate protein measurement becomes critically important.  Unfortunately, commercially available NF1 antibodies (both polyclonal and monoclonal) have been shown to have significant limitations, including the inability to use these antibodies in ELISA and IHC applications. Utilizing full-length neurofibromin (isolated and purified by the Frank McCormick lab and Dominic Esposito’s team at the Frederick National Lab) as the immunogen, and leveraging a proprietary antibody development platform, Alicanto©, from Digital Proteomics, LLC, the San Diego-based team at Infixion Bioscience set out to develop a new and improved monoclonal antibody against NF1. Project goals include:      identifying a mAb with increased sensitivity and specificity against neurofibromin as determined by western blot, and     demonstrate expanded utility with function in ELISAs, sandwich ELISAs and immunohistochemistry (IHC) applications.  Additional collaborating partners on the project included: Dr. Michael Frost (IHC development), Dr. Dominic Esposito (epitope mapping), and Dr. Eduard Serra Lab (characterization in NF1 iPSC lines).

studyName: Ultra-low-pass whole genome sequencing of plasma cfDNA from patients with plexiform neurofibroma and malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors
summary: The leading cause of mortality for patients with the Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) cancer predisposition syndrome is development of Malignant Peripheral Nerve Sheath Tumor (MPNST), an aggressive soft tissue sarcoma. In the setting of NF1, this aggressive cancer frequently arises in histologically benign plexiform neurofibroma (PN). However, transformation from the benign PN to MPNST can be challenging to diagnose due to equivocal imaging results and intralesional heterogeneity resulting in biopsy sampling errors. This multi-institution study used ultra-low-pass whole genome sequencing (ULP-WGS) of plasma cell-free DNA (cfDNA) to distinguish between MPNST and PN neoplasms in patients with NF1.

studyName: Evaluating genetic modifiers of cutaneous neurofibromas in adults with Neurofibromatosis Type 1
summary: The manifestations of NF1 are highly variable between affected individuals. Greater than 2800 pathogenic variants in the NF1 gene are associated with NF1, however, only a very small number of NF1 variants have been associated with a predictable phenotype. These associations include a severe disease burden in the case of a constitutional NF1 microdeletion and missense mutations of codons 844 to 848 versus milder manifestations associated with missense mutation codon Arg 1809 or a single amino acid deletion at position 2971.1,2 These mutations occur in an exceedingly rare number of patients, but illustrate the potential value of genotype-phenotype discovery for both clinical care (re: prognosis and recommended surveillance) as well as in selecting patient populations most likely to benefit from various therapeutic approaches in development.  Multiple challenges have contributed to the limited number of identified genotype-phenotype correlations. These include the age dependency of many manifestations in NF1, the timing and number of second hits in different cells, and wide NF1 allelic heterogeneity. Advances in understanding the relationship between genotype and clinical manifestations is critical to personalizing therapeutic development for both individual manifestations of NF1 and optimizing clinical management of genetically classified subpopulations of people with NF1. This proposal seeks to investigate modifier genes that are present in adults with NF1 with high versus low burden of cutaneous neurofibromas (cNF). Our overall goal is to evaluate the genetic basis of the variability in burden of cNF in people with NF1 in order to facilitate new therapeutic development for cNF and advancing the understanding about the variability of NF1.
