studyName: DNA methylation signatures in peripheral leukocytes of patients with Schwannomatosis or sporadic schwannoma
summary: Aberrant DNA methylation is associated with cancer development and progression. There are several types of specimens from which DNA methylation patterns can be measured and evaluated as an indicator of disease status (from normal biological process to pathologic condition) and even of pharmacologic response to therapy. Blood-based specimens such as cell-free circulating nucleic acid and DNA extracted from leukocytes in peripheral blood may be a potential source of non-invasive cancer biomarkers. As part of our synodos for schwannomatosis study we focused on multiplatform genomic analysis of schwannomatosis related schwannomas. We also performed DNA methylation profiling on whole genomic DNA isolated from peripheral blood leukocytes from 27 schwannomatosis patients and 22 patients with sporadic non-syndromic schwannomas. This analysis was outside the scope of the synodos for schwannomatosis study; however, we were interested in evaluating the proportion of immune cell types in the blood of patients with peripheral nerve sheath tumors including schwannomatosis patients. After performing QC analysis, we removed 5 schwannomatosis samples (failed QC: detp>0.05). We then Removed 176834 failed probes (detp>0.05), 12613 probes on the X and Y sex chromosomes, 23507 probes associated with SNPs at the CpG sites, and 24267 cross-reactive probes. Total 630553 probes were left for clustering analysis. We then performed cell deconvolution analysis using IDOLOptimizedCpGs method  to determine the proportion of immune cell types in blood of patients with schwannomatosis or non-syndromic sporadic schwannomas including neutrophils, monocytes, CD4 T cells, CD8 T cells, B cells and NK cells. We then clustered the samples based on immune cell proportions. We found that schwannomatosis samples clustered separate from sporadic schwannomas. Our results suggested that schwannomatosis patients harboured a higher neutrophil to lymphocyte ratio (NLR) compared to schwannomas. Further studies are required to determine the clinical implications of this result, in addition to continued work to uncover the biological underpinnings of these differences among these syndromic and non-syndromic disorders.

studyName: Whole Body MRI of NF Patients
summary: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is the most common diagnostic imaging modality for longitudinal monitoring of patients with Neurofibromatosis 1 (NF1), NF2, and schwannomatosis. Because NF tumors can be extensive and occurring anywhere in the body, whole-body MRI (WBMRI), instead of regional MRI, is recommended as the standard imaging modality for longitudinal evaluating of NF patients. However, conventional linear tumor measurement, such as bi-diameter (WHO) or single diameter (RECIST), is less sensitive and less reliable to measure the growth rate of irregularly shaped NF tumors that grow in non-uniform ways. Hence, measurement of tumor volume is a key component in estimating tumor burden in NF patients. For NF tumor volumetrics in MRI, image segmentation can be challenging, as the lesions are irregular and complex, and there may be many lesions in a patient. Efficient and reliable tumor volumetric segmentation methods are needed for the assessment of the patient tumor burden including the number, size (volume), location (body part), and type (discrete or plexiform) of NF tumors carried by a patient.

studyName: Defining the factors that dictate the pattern of glioma formation in NF1
summary: Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) is a cancer predisposition syndrome caused by a wide spectrum of germline mutations in the NF1 gene. Children with NF1 have a ~20% risk of developing low-grade brain tumors of the optic pathway (optic pathway glioma; OPG) or brainstem (brainstem glioma; BSG). However, it is currently unclear which children with NF1 will develop these brain tumors. Emerging human population-based evidence has raised the possibility that patient-specific risk factors, including infant birth weight and the specific germline NF1 mutation that each child is born with, may modulate the risk of glioma development. High-infant birth weight can be modeled in mice by maternal exposure to a high-fat high-sucrose (HFHS) diet. Based on my preliminary data demonstrating that both germline mutation and maternal HFHS diet increase proliferation and glial differentiation of specific neuroglial progenitor (NPC) populations, I now hypothesize that both disease-intrinsic factors (different germline NF1 gene mutations; Aim 1) and disease-extrinsic factors (maternal HFHS diet; Aim 2) act on spatially-defined populations of NPCs to modulate NF1-glioma penetrance. In this grant, I will determine whether specific germline Nf1 mutations affect the proliferation and differentiation of NPCs from different ventricular surfaces over the course of mouse brain development (Aim 1) and whether maternal HFHS diet exposure modifies these responses (Aim 2). Taken together, these experiments aim to determine whether germline NF1 gene mutations and maternal diet function as risk factors for NF1-glioma formation in different regions of the brain.

studyName: Defining the RABL6A-YAP axis in MPNST pathogenesis and therapy
summary: MPNSTs represent one of the most aggressive and clinically challenging subtypes of sarcoma. The only known cure for MPNST is complete surgical resection with adjuvant radiation and/or chemotherapy. Unfortunately, surgery is often not feasible due to the location and/or size of the tumors, and traditional radiation and chemotherapy does not reduce patient mortality. NF1 patients are at increased risk of MPNST development compared to the general population due to transformation of plexiform neurofibromas (~one-third), and MPNSTs are the leading cause of death in these patients. Although our understanding of neurofibroma (NF) transformation and MPNST biology has significantly increased in recent years, effective treatment for these deadly tumors is still lacking. My thesis studies centered on understanding the contributions of RABL6A, a potent oncoprotein, to MPNST pathogenesis in an effort to develop meaningful, effective therapies for patients. We demonstrated RABL6A negatively regulates the retinoblastoma (RB1) tumor suppressor, a key pathway known to be disrupted during the transformation of NFs-to-MPNSTs. Further, we and others have found RABL6A promotes MEK signaling, another important pathway driving NF1-associated MPNST development. Gene expression microarray studies suggest RABL6A controls many cancer-promoting pathways, only a few of which have been investigated. While the pre-malignant transition from NF to an intermediate lesion (ANNUBP) appears to occur with few genetic alterations, MPNSTs are highly complex with numerous chromosomal gains and losses. The key alterations required for MPNST development are not known, highlighting a major knowledge gap in the field. Our long-term goal is to define essential molecular events promoting MPNST development to identify new therapeutic targets and establish more effective therapy options for patients. We recently discovered that inhibitors of CDK4/6 (RB1 negative regulator) combined with MEK inhibitors synergistically combats MPNST growth in vivo. The combination dramatically delayed tumor progression and increased mouse survival by more than 3-fold. However, drug resistance inevitably occurred, emphasizing the need for additional targeted therapies. Preliminary data suggest RABL6A is a new regulator of YAP, another oncoprotein whose hyperactivity has recently been implicated in MPNSTs. Further, induction of YAP activity has been linked to CDK4/6 and MEK inhibitor resistance in other cancers. Our objective in this proposal is to elucidate the mechanistic link between RABL6A and YAP in MPNST and evaluate the efficacy of RABL6A-YAP targeted therapy. Our central hypothesis is that RABL6A and YAP act cooperatively to drive MPNST pathogenesis and represent clinically meaningful targets for therapy. In Aim 1, we will define the specific molecular connections and functional importance of RABL6A-YAP signaling in MPNSTs using patient specimens and cell line models. The hypothesis to be tested is that YAP activation by RABL6A drives MPNST pathogenesis. In Aim 2, we will determine the pathobiological significance and therapeutic value of targeting the RABL6A-YAP axis in MPNSTs using genetic editing and de novo tumor models. The hypothesis to be tested is that combination targeting of the RABL6A-YAP axis will be highly synergistic against MPNSTs and abrogate drug resistance. By elucidating the mechanisms and biological relevance of RABL6A-YAP regulation and targeting in MPNSTs, we expect to improve the therapeutic options for patients suffering from this deadly disease.

studyName: Targeting the Let7-HMGA2 axis in Malignant Peripheral Nerve Sheath Tumor Prevention
summary: Malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors (MPNST) are incurable sarcomas that represent the leading cause of death in NF1 patients. Developing therapeutic strategies to not only treat MPNST, but ultimately to prevent their occurrence is paramount to improve survival, reduce suffering, and alleviate the burden of care for persons with NF1. Our laboratory has developed genetically engineered mouse (GEM) models that accurately phenocopy the development of MPNST from plexiform (PN) and atypical neurofibroma (ANNUBP) precursor tumors, thus allowing for interrogation of interventions that can both treat as well as prevent MPNST. These GEM models have led to the identification of an oncofetal microRNA-protein axis (Let7- HMGA2) that undergoes profound alteration in both murine and human PN/ANNUBP as these tumors progress to MPNST. We hypothesize that Let7-HMGA2 deregulation reprograms broad transcriptional and kinase networks to drive MPNST progression by reactivating programs of embryonic growth in their tumor initiating cells of origin. By isolating this unique population of cancer stem cells from the embryonic nerve roots, we will systematically characterize how Let7-HMGA2 perturbation alters broad networks of protein kinases and transcription factors to drive the aggressive behavior of these tumors. Furthermore, through both genetic and pharmacologic methods, we will establish whether HMGA2 inhibition can treat and/or prevent the progression of MPNST from PN and ANNUBP precursor tumors in vivo. If this is confirmed, we will have identified a targetable pathway to prevent the occurrence of these devastating tumors by controlling and eradicating early clones of disease in a vulnerable population of at risk patients.")

studyName: Towards clinical translation of imaging studies in neurofibromatosis type 1
summary: Ras/mitogen-activated protein kinase (RMK) pathway is central for brain development and function. In children with neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1), genetic mutations affecting the RMK pathway lead to multisystemic disorder, including measurable effects on behavior and cognition. Mainly, NF1 increases the risk of deficits in attention, hyperactivity, and social skills. While the effects of NF1 on human brain structure and function are evident, their usability as outcome measures is limited. Using high-resolution structural MRI, diffusion-weighted imaging, resting-state fMRI, (neural correlates) and a targeted battery of cognitive-behavioral assessments, we will first assess the neural correlates of, and cognitive-behavioral features associated with attentional and social dysfunction in children with NF1 relative to controls. Then, we will leverage recent advances in brain imaging techniques and computational methods; we will assess the effect of NF1 on the organization and coupling of large-scale structural and functional brain networks. We hypothesize that NF1 is associated with abnormal organization of brain networks implicated in attention and social skills. Our sample will include 30 children with NF1 seen at 5-11 years of age. We will compare them to 30 sex- and age-matched typically developing controls as well as to a (clinical) group of 30 age-matched children with Noonan syndrome (NS). The inclusion of a clinical control group (NS) that is caused by a different genetic mutation related to the RMK pathway will enable us to define a specific profile of brain-based correlates of neurodevelopmental disabilities in children with NF1. The rationale for the proposed project is that defining the brain organization and characterizing the coupling between brain structure and function in NF1 holds promise for providing novel brain-based outcome measures for future clinical interventions in NF1.

studyName: Single cell sequencing of glioma in NF1 patients
summary: The study aims to the characterization of the intra-tumor heterogeneity and microenvironment of glioma occurring in neurofibromatosis 1 (NF1) patients by profiling individual cells using single cell RNA sequencing. We performed individual cell level analyses using single-nucleus RNA-sequencing (Nucseq). Nucseq allows the analysis of frozen tumor specimens, the only currently banked NF1 glioma specimens. We note that profiling of tissue by Nucseq does not require tissue dissociation and has therefore the advantage of preserving the cell types that could be lost during the dissociation process (i.e. more fragile cell types). Single-nucleus molecular profiling allows to dissect the complex architecture underlying glioma subclonal heterogeneity as well as to characterize the tumor microenvironment. We were particularly interested in the identification of subpopulations reflecting neuronal or glial differentiation or their progenitors, as this may uncover the cell-of-origin, cancer stem cell, and potential avenues for differentiation. We evaluated the role of genetic heterogeneity in generating transcriptionally-distinct subpopulations by analyzing mutations (identified in single cell RNA-Seq reads), and chromosomal aberrations (inferred from expression of contiguous sets of genes) to define genetic sub-clones and examine the link between genetics and transcriptional programs. By generating single cell resolution data with minimal technical confounders, we highlighted the oncogenic programs unique to NF1 glioma and candidate vulnerabilities of defined NF1 glioma sub-classes.

studyName: Evaluation of the use of antisense oligonucleotides as a personalized therapy for Neurofibromatosis Type 2 patients
summary: Background: Neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2) is a genetic condition characterized by the development of multiple tumors of the nervous system. The clinical presentation of the disease is variable and related to the type of the inherited constitutional mutation variant in the NF2 gene. The use of antisense oligonucleotides (AONs), acting at RNA level, could be useful to correct the effect of deleterious DNA mutations at the protein level, or to create proteins that still retain partial function from loss-of-function mutated alleles. AONs They could be used to force the skipping of exons carrying truncating mutations when the reading frame is maintained. We have shown that a deep intronic mutation responsible for an aberrant NF2 splicing could be corrected by the use of PMOs and recover Merlin function. Here, we propose to evaluate the use of AONs PMOs to reduce the severity of NF2 truncating and splicing mutations to milder hypomorphic forms in vitro.   Methods: Samples: primary fibroblasts cultures from NF2 patients. Phosphorodiamidate morpholino oligomers (PMOs)AONs: We designed specific phosphorodiamidate morpholino oligomers (PMOs) targeting four independent disease-causing splicing mutationsvariants, and a pair of PMOs to induce exon skipping of exons 4, 6&7, 8, and 11 of the NF2 gene. Primary fibroblasts carrying nonsense mutations variants were treated with the corresponding pair of PMOs. A dose-response and a time course study were performed to set-up conditions and confirmed the in-frame skipping of the target exons by RT-PCR and Sanger sequencing. Functional analysis: Functional studies were performed from fibroblast cultures untreated and treated at different PMOs concentrations. We measured: 1) Merlin, ERK and their phosphorylated forms by Western Blot; 2) actin cytoskeleton organization; 3) NF2 and YAP1 nuclear translocation capacity by immunofluorescence, and 4) proliferation capacity.   Results: MutationVariant-specific PMOs for splicing mutations: our results showed the PMOs designed for splicing variants located at +/- 15 (or less) from the intron-exon boundary region, were not specific enough and interfered in the correct splicing signaling of both wild-type and mutated alleles. Exon-specific PMOs for truncating mutationsvariants: the effect of the exon skipping on both the mutated and the WT allele, although maintaining the NF2 gene reading frame at cDNA level, caused the complete loss of Merlin. Despite these results, complementary functional analysis are being performed to confirm the absence of Merlin at a cellular level.  Conclusions: PMOs might be optimal for inducing targeted exon skipping without altering gene transcription in cells carrying deep intronic variants, or for the modulation of alternative spliced exons. However, here we show that, in the case of NF2, PMOs may not be useful for correcting splicing when mutations are located in splicing canonical sites, neither for inducing semi-functional Merlin isoforms, since the use of these antisense molecules results in total Merlin loss

studyName: Signaling pathways regulated by nitrated proteins as novel therapeutic targets for neurofibromatosis type 2
summary: Neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2) is a genetic disorder caused by inactivating mutations in the gene encoding the tumor suppressor merlin. NF2 patients develop schwannomas, meningiomas, and ependymomas throughout their life. NF2 patients have few therapeutic options; given the chronic and recurring nature of NF2, careful monitoring and resection radio surgery remains the treatment of choice. Further understanding the drivers of cell proliferation in NF2 and identifying new potential therapeutic targets remains paramount to improve the selectivity of drugs intended for the treatment of these chronic, recurrent tumors. Our group made a fundamental discovery: production of the powerful oxidant peroxynitrite and subsequent tyrosine (Tyr) nitration, an oxidative modification to proteins that occurs in pathological conditions, are essential for NF2 schwannoma cell survival. Excitingly, protein Tyr nitration is very low or absent in healthy cells. Our published and preliminary data posit nitrated proteins as a new category of tumor-directed targets for the development of tumor-directed therapies. We are determined to identify the role of nitrated proteins in the pathogenesis of NF2 and propose Tyr nitrated proteins are a novel therapeutic target. We have identified a number of proteins that are endogenously nitrated in vestibular schwannomas (VS) from NF2 patients. Six of these nitrated proteins are directly involved in signaling pathways dysregulated by the loss of merlin: Galectin 1 (Gal-1), Ras homolog family member A (RhoA), RhoC, Ras related protein 35, 14-3-3, Vimentin and Heat shock protein 90 (Hsp90). We discovered that nitrated Hsp90 supports schwannoma cell survival through a gain-of-function, but we also discovered that Hsp90 is not the only nitrated protein with pro-tumorigenic functions, and these other players remain unidentified. Therefore, the goals of the project are to 1) determine the regulation of signaling pathways by Tyr nitration in general, and Tyr nitrated Hsp90 in particular; and 2) identify the specific nitrated protein(s) that support NF2 tumor cell survival, providing a wealth of novel information and opening the door to the development of new therapies for NF2 treatment.

studyName: Targeting inflammatory signaling in cutaneous neurofibromas
summary: Cutaneous (CNF) and plexiform neurofibromas (PNF) are defining features of Neurofibromatosis Type 1 (NF1), accounting for substantial morbidity and mortality across the age spectrum. Although histologically similar, CNFs and PNFs exhibit vastly different clinical behavior as they demonstrate distinct growth rates, anatomic sites of presentation, and malignant potential. The reasons for this disparate clinical behavior are not well explained by genome or transcriptome profiling studies. We recently demonstrated that CNFs and PNFs are epigenetically distinct neoplasms that exhibit genome-wide differences in chromatin conformation and site-specific methylation events (SSMEs) such as differentially methylated regions (DMRs). Collectively, these methylation events altered genes involved in key biological processes, particularly the coupling of inflammatory and RAS signaling. Epigenetic reinforcement of RAS/MKK/p38 was a defining characteristic of CNFs leading to pro-inflammatory signaling and transient receptor potential (TRP) pain receptor regulation, whereas PNFs signaled predominantly through RAS/MEK. This difference is clearly demonstrated in the downstream RAS/p38 signaling effector, COX2.  In the COX2 gene, PTGS2, we identified a DMR near the promoter that was significantly hypomethylated in CNFs compared to PNFs, with the strongest hypomethylation present in symptomatic CNFs. These data confirm that 1) CNFs are epigenetically distinct from PNFs, 2) treatment of CNFs will require targeting signaling pathways outside of or parallel to RAS/MEK such as inflammatory pathways, and 3) RAS signaling fates downstream of NF1 are strongly under epigenetic control. Our goal is to develop effective and sustainable treatments for CNFs, as well as practical diagnostic tools. To do this, we will define how the methylation and chromatin conformation states of key regulatory genes affect CNF growth, symptoms, response to MEK inhibitors and other novel CNF therapies. Our overarching hypothesis is that inflammatory signaling plays a critical role in CNF symptom evolution and tumor growth that is determined both by SSMEs and p38-mediated chromatin conformation changes (i.e. �epigenetic reinforcement�). To test this hypothesis we will establish an inflammatory pain signature by comparing the methylation profiles of symptomatic and asymptomatic CNFs, and in a correlative study determine if treatment with the topical COX2 inhibitor, diclofenac, can reverse this inflammatory pain signature in patients with symptomatic CNFs. At the same time, we will strategically collect additional untreated tumor and normal tissue from patients and unaffected first-degree relatives for patient derived explants (PDEs) that model human CNFs or skin in culture. Using PDEs we will determine how NF1 loss poises the skin microenvironment to support CNF formation and drive pain signaling in response to environmental inflammatory stimuli. We will also evaluate several novel therapeutic targets using CNF PDEs, including MAPK modulators (p38, DUSP, MEK) as well as epigenetic treatments (5-Azacytidine) to determine if they can reverse epigenetic reinforcement of inflammatory pain signaling ex vivo. Finally, we will use the epigenomic data generated in this study as a validation cohort against a CNF/PNF SSME-based biomarker prediction panel assembled from our previous study and several publicly available data sets. Collectively, this work will establish the biological efficacy of topical COX2 inhibition for treatment of CNFs, evaluate novel CNF therapeutic targets preclinically, elucidate how NF1 loss and epigenetic reinforcement of inflammatory signaling supports CNF growth and symptom evolution, and design and test an epigenetic biomarker panel for CNFs. As a result, our proposal will greatly advance CNF diagnosis and treatment for NF1 patients.

studyName: Understanding how epigenetic dysregulation and Ras misactivation cooperate during NF1 deficient Schwann cell tumorigenesis to driven druggable dependencies
summary: Neural crest derived Schwann cells give rise to neurofibromas, schwannomas, and MPNSTs. Despite their shared embryonic origin, the clinical course of these tumors is quite different. Neurofibromas and schwannomas are benign lesions that are well managed with local therapy while MPNSTs are aggressive tumors that metastasize and have poor outcomes.1 MPNSTs can arise from neurofibromas or schwannomas following malignant transformation in the setting of NF1 loss or ionizing radiation.2�5 NF1 encodes a tumor suppressor that inhibits Ras signaling, a conserved pathway required for development and misactivated in 1/3 of cancers6 including Schwann cell derived tumors.7 However, only a minority of neurofibromas and schwannomas progress to MPNSTs, suggesting additional steps are required. In addition to NF1, MPNSTs harbor mutations in the Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2),8�10 a chromatin modifier which regulates gene repression in development and cancer via H3K27 trimethylation.11 My objective is to elucidate how epigenetic mechanisms contribute to malignant transformation in Ras activated tumors.

studyName: Exploiting cytotoxic role of nuclear Rac1 to develop targeted antitumor therapy of NF2-associated tumor
summary: Neurofibromatosis type II (NF2) is a genetic disorder characterized by the development of multiple tumors in central nervous system. NF2 is an autosomal dominant genetic disease caused by mutation appearance in NF2 gene, i.e. if a child, a boy or a girl, is unlucky to born with such mutation then the disease will develop with a probability of almost 100%. There is no any specific treatment for NF2 just only non-specific radiotherapy and surgery but sometimes that methods are useless due to remote localization of tumor. Our proposal is to use statins and bisphosphonates for treating NF2 patients because the mechanism of their action is based on specific features of NF2 tumors. Furthermore we propose to use statins and bisphophonates jointly because in our previous studies we have established that the mechanism of action of each compound affect the same process in cell but in different stages and both compounds slowed down the growth of NF2-tumors in preclinical studies. These data demonstrates that joint using of statins and bisphosphonates have ability to enhance effects of each other that may lead to decreasing size of NF2-associated tumors. In our studies already approved drugs are used which safety is proved (simvastatin, lovastatin belonging to statin, zolderonic acid belonging to bisphosphonates). Our proposal suggests to use difference in activity of the protein Rac1 between cells of NF2-associated tumors and normal cells as target for specific pharmaceutical therapy. Rac1 activity is increased in NF2 tumor cells compared to normal cells. It is a pivotal step for development of this approach which will allow to move on preclinical stuides with laboratory animals. We hope that results obtained in our studies could be used for cure NF2-patients.

studyName: Neural Underpinnings of Attention in Children with NF1
summary: Attention difficulties are one of the most apparent aspects of the cognitive phenotype of neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1), yet very little is known about the underlying neural mechanisms of attention in children with NF1. Children with NF1 have difficulties with various aspects of attention, including sustained, divided, shifting, visual, and auditory (Casnar & Klein-Tasman, 2017; Isenberg et al., 2013; North et al., 2002).  While some children with NF1 show attention difficulties that meet criteria for Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), there are also children whose difficulties do not meet that threshold but who nevertheless still demonstrate marked difficulties with sustained attention (Mautner et al., 2001) and planning (Hyman et al., 2005). Research in other populations, such as ADHD, has begun elucidating specific biomarkers of attention difficulties using electroencephalography (EEG) Event Related Potentials (ERPs). EEG is a relatively affordable and non-invasive imaging technique that can be used to further delineate neural mechanisms of attention difficulties. However, very few studies have used EEG methodology to examine the neural underpinnings of these attention difficulties in children with NF1. The goal of this research is to demonstrate the feasibility and promise of EEG approaches with school age children with NF1 to identify potential biomarkers of attention problems. While there is considerable variability in the behavioral phenotype of NF1, attention problems are commonly identified. There is a dearth of research about the neural underpinnings of these challenges, especially with school age children.   There is a need to identify biomarkers of attention difficulties in children with neurofibromatosis type 1 to effectively track the impact of medical and psychosocial interventions that affect attention in NF1. Research shows that many youth with NF1 experience attention problems (Huijbregts et al., 2010; Templer et al., 2013), which are evident on performance-based, caregiver and teacher report measures (Casnar & Klein-Tasman, 2017), however, the neural underpinnings of attention problems in children with NF1 have not yet been sufficiently characterized. This may be important for identifying potential biomarkers of attention difficulties, and eventually neural underpinnings of attention in children with NF1 by understanding the impact of interventions (including medications) on attention and related brain function. Unique EEG patterns may provide researchers with an NF1-specific index of attention difficulties at the neural level rather than based on questionnaire and neuropsychological task performance measures. Further, there is evidence from other populations that changes in the neural underpinnings may in fact be evident prior to behavioral changes; for example, in Social Phobia, reduced activity in the amygdala and limbic regions of the brain may be a “prerequisite” for behavioral improvement (Ribeiro Porto et al., 2009). Such evidence is also present in studies of children with ADHD, which has led a task force to recommend continued research into neurophysiological methods, such as ERPs, as biomarkers in ADHD (Thome et al., 2012). And, indeed, research about the utility of ERPs as biomarkers has also been expanded to other populations that are affected by ADHD, such as Tuberous Sclerosis Complex (Moavero et al., 2020). Thus, extending this work to NF1, which has considerable overlap with ADHD, is warranted.  We will examine attention in 7 through 11-year-olds with NF1 using a multi-method approach. This includes caregiver questionnaires about attention, performance-based measures of attention administered by trained staff evaluators, and Event Related Potentials (ERPs) ascertained through electroencephalography (EEG). We will use a Flanker task and a Go/Nogo task, which are known to elicit our components of interest: N2, P3, and ERN. The N2 and P3 components are indices of visual selective attention to salient stimuli. Error-Related Negativity (ERN) appears in response to making an error of inhibition. Our sample will include 20 children diagnosed with NF1, 20 children diagnosed with idiopathic Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), and 20 unaffected children without both NF1 and ADHD. The groups will be matched by age and sex. We have chosen a narrow age range because developmental EEG studies suggest that there is considerable age-related variability in some ERP components; the broad age range of studies to date of children with NF1 might obscure developmental effects.   Aim 1 is to examine group differences in ERP measures of attention. Our aim is to identify neural underpinnings of attention problems in school age children with NF1 in comparison to a clinical contrast group of children with ADHD and a control group of children without both NF1 and ADHD. We hypothesize that compared to same-aged unaffected children, children with NF1 will show a reduced, and potentially delayed, N2 and P3 to incongruent Flanker and Nogo trials, and a reduced error-related negativity (ERN) following errors on both tasks. We also hypothesize that compared to same-aged children with ADHD, children with NF1 will show different patterns of N2, P3, and ERN activity. Aim 2 is to examine relations between specific ERP components and behavioral indicators of attention problems in children with NF1. We will examine the relations between components (N2, P3, and ERN) that show group differences with behavioral indicators of attention problems, including both performance-based and caregiver-report measures. We will also examine any differences in the patterns of relations between groups. We hypothesize that reduced amplitude and latency will be related to poorer attention on both performance-based and caregiver-report measures.

studyName: Pilot Study of Factors Impacting Medication Adherence in Children, Adolescents, and Adults with Neurofibromatosis Type 1 (NF1) on Clinical Treatment Trials
summary: Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) is a genetic disorder. It has a broad variety of effects on the body. Up to half of people with NF1 get plexiform neurofibromas (PNs). These are benign tumors. But they can have serious effects like pain and disfigurement. To treat PNs, a person may have to take medicine every day for a long period of time. Researchers think that it will be important for people to take the medicine regularly for it to work. They want to study how well people with NF1 follow their treatment plan for PNs. Objective: To study how often people with neurofibromatosis type 1 take medicine that has been prescribed to them for treating plexiform neurofibromas. Eligibility: People ages 18–59 already enrolled in an NF1 clinical trial. Design: Participants will need access to the internet to do the study activities. Participants will complete baseline questionnaires assessing demographic data, recent life events, how much pain interferes with daily life, ability to focus and pay attention to tasks, and emotional distress or depression. Through 18 months, participants will mark down every time they take a dose of the medicine in their clinical trial on a provided daily diary. The pill bottles they get in their trial will have a chip in the cap that will record when it is opened. Their returned pills will also be counted at clinical trial visits. Participants will also answer a series of questions about adherence in qualitive interviews with a study team member and fill out a measure assessing barriers to adherence upon study completion. Expected accrual is 12-15 participants.
